claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels drain the CNS to the deep cervical lymph nodes in mice.
source: Mouse studies have demonstrated that meningeal lymphatic vessels convey macromolecules and immune cells from the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) to the deep cervical lymph nodes (Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Louveau et al., 2018b

claim: CD11c+ cells accumulate in the dural meninges of mice chronically infected with T. gondii ME49 strain.
source: Supporting a role for these cells in the immune response to brain infection, we report a striking accumulation of CD11c+ cells in the dural meninges of CD11cYFP reporter mice chronically infected with the ME49 strain of T. gondii (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy imaging data shown in Figure 1a

claim: CD11c+ cells localize preferentially around the dural sinuses near meningeal lymphatic vessels in chronically infected mice.
source: CD11c+ cells localized preferentially around the dural sinuses near meningeal lymphatic vessels (Figure 1b), increasing local area coverage from 9% in naïve mice to 44% in chronically infected mice (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 1b and 1c

claim: The number of CD11c+ cells co-localized to LYVE1+ meningeal lymphatic vessels increases threefold in chronically infected mice compared to naïve mice.
source: This accumulation of CD11c+ cells around the sinuses was associated with a threefold increase in the number of CD11c+ cells co-localized to LYVE1+ meningeal lymphatic vessels in infected mice compared to naïve mice (Figure 1d–e).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 1d-e

claim: There is a threefold increase in the number of cDC1s in the dural meninges at 6 weeks post-infection compared to naïve and acutely infected mice.
source: While there was no difference in the number of cDC1s (CD45+Lin-CD11chiMHC IIhiCD64-CD26+XCR1+SIRPα-) or cDC2s (CD45+Lin-CD11chiMHC IIhiCD64-CD26+XCR1-SIRPα+) in naive and acutely infected mice, by 6 weeks post-infection (wpi) there was a threefold increase in the number of cDC1s and sixfold increase in the number of cDC2s in the dural meninges (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: Supported by spectral flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1f

claim: There is a sixfold increase in the number of cDC2s in the dural meninges at 6 weeks post-infection compared to naïve and acutely infected mice.
source: While there was no difference in the number of cDC1s (CD45+Lin-CD11chiMHC IIhiCD64-CD26+XCR1+SIRPα-) or cDC2s (CD45+Lin-CD11chiMHC IIhiCD64-CD26+XCR1-SIRPα+) in naive and acutely infected mice, by 6 weeks post-infection (wpi) there was a threefold increase in the number of cDC1s and sixfold increase in the number of cDC2s in the dural meninges (Figure 1f–g).
evidence: Supported by spectral flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1g

claim: Parasite burden in the brain peaks at 6 weeks post-infection.
source: Intriguingly, the expansion of the dendritic cell compartment in the dural meninges during chronic infection tracked with increasing parasite burden in the brain, which was found to peak at 6 wpi by real-time PCR (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 1h

claim: Parasite could not be detected in the dural meninges at 6 weeks post-infection by real-time PCR or immunostaining.
source: By contrast, parasite could not be detected in the dural meninges at 6 wpi by either real-time PCR or immunostaining of PFA-fixed tissue (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR data in Figure 1h and immunostaining in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d

claim: cDC2s display broader upregulation of co-stimulatory molecules and MHC class II compared to cDC1s during chronic infection.
source: Additionally, cDC2s displayed a much broader degree of activation compared to cDC1s, upregulating expression of CD80, CD86, and MHC class II (Figure 1i–k).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1i-k

claim: cDC1s express minimal levels of CD80 during chronic infection.
source: By contrast, cDC1s expressed minimal levels of CD80 (Figure 1i) and showed an increase in CD86 expression but not MHC class II expression (Figure 1j–k).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1i

claim: cDC1s show an increase in CD86 expression but not MHC class II expression during chronic infection.
source: By contrast, cDC1s expressed minimal levels of CD80 (Figure 1i) and showed an increase in CD86 expression but not MHC class II expression (Figure 1j–k).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1j-k

claim: A population of CD11chiMHC IIhi APCs emerges in the CSF of chronically infected mice that is not present in naïve mice.
source: Notably, 46% of OT-I cells displayed complete dilution in the DCLNs when mice were infected with Pru-OVA, compared to only 11% of OT-I cells when mice were infected with parental Pru (Figure 6i–j).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3a-b

claim: Within 2 hours of intra-cisterna magna injection, 30% of cDC1s and cDC2s in the dural meninges harbor DQ-OVA cleavage products.
source: Within 2 hr of i.c.m. injection, we found that 30% of cDC1s and cDC2s in the dural meninges harbored DQ-OVA cleavage products (Figure 1—figure supplement 2h-j).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2h-j

claim: After 24 hours of intra-cisterna magna injection, approximately 5% of cDC1s and cDC2s harbor DQ-OVA cleavage products.
source: After 24 hr, cleavage products were detected in ~5% of cDC1s and cDC2s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2h-j), which may reflect egress of DQ-OVA +dendritic cells from the meninges or loss of the BODIPY fluorescent signal over time.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2h-j

claim: DQ-OVA+ cells are distributed along and within lymphatic vessels after 12 hours of intra-cisterna magna injection.
source: Imaging of whole mount dural meninges revealed that DQ-OVA+ cells were distributed along and within lymphatic vessels after 12 hr, suggesting that dural APCs capture and transport CSF-borne antigen during chronic brain infection (Figure 1m).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1m

claim: Upon intra-cisterna magna injection of DQ-OVA into chronically infected mice, 3% of CD11chiMHC IIhi APCs in the DCLNs harbor digested protein products after 5 hours.
source: Upon i.c.m. injection of DQ-OVA into chronically infected mice, 3% of CD11chiMHC IIhi APCs in the DCLNs were found to harbor digested protein products after 5 hr (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2a-b

claim: Processed DQ-OVA is not detected in the inguinal lymph nodes after intra-cisterna magna injection.
source: By contrast, processed DQ-OVA was not detected in the inguinal lymph nodes (ILN), which drain peripheral tissue (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2a-b

claim: Equal proportions of cDC1s and cDC2s harbor digested DQ-OVA protein products at both 2 hours and 24 hours after intra-cisterna magna injection.
source: Further characterization of the DQ-OVA+ APC populations in the DCLNs revealed that equal proportions of cDC1s and cDC2s harbored digested protein products both at 2 hr and 24 hr after i.c.m. injection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-c), the latter time point representing when migratory dendritic cells trafficking from the meninges have been shown to reach the DCLNs (Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-c

claim: The peak in number of activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs occurs at 6-8 weeks post-infection.
source: Expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs became more pronounced after progression to the chronic stage of infection, with the peak in number of activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells occurring at 6–8 wpi (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2c-d

claim: The peak SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cell response in the ILNs occurs during acute infection (2-3 weeks post-infection).
source: Consistent with the polyclonal CD8+ T cell response observed in response to ME49 infection (Figure 2d), the peak SIINFKEKL-specific CD8+ T cell response in the ILNs occurred during acute infection (2–3 wpi), when very few parasite-specific T cells were detectable in the DCLNs (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Expansion of parasite-specific CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs is greatest during chronic infection, increasing significantly between 3 and 6 weeks post-infection.
source: By contrast, expansion of parasite-specific CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs was greatest during chronic infection, increasing significantly between 3 and 6 wpi (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 2e

claim: Parasite-specific T cell responses in the DCLNs track with parasite burden in the brain.
source: These results likely reflect the distinct sources of antigen that each lymph node site drains during the different stages of infection. In support of this, we found that parasite-specific T cell responses in the DCLNs tracked with parasite burden in the brain (Figure 2f), whereas parasite-specific T cell responses in the ILNs tracked with parasite burden in the ILNs.
evidence: Supported by correlation between T cell response data and parasite burden data shown in Figure 2f

claim: Ligation surgery results in a greater than 95% reduction in outflow of CSF-derived components to the DCLNs.
source: Tracer studies using Evans blue or Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated ovalbumin (OVA-AF594) confirmed the efficacy of the procedure and demonstrated a greater than 95% reduction in outflow of CSF-derived components to the DCLNs in ligated animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b).
evidence: Supported by tracer studies shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b

claim: Ligation does not affect outflow of CSF to the superficial cervical lymph nodes.
source: Importantly, ligation did not affect outflow of CSF to the superficial cervical lymph nodes, another drainage site for CSF-borne protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c; Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by tracer studies shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and citation to Ma et al., 2017

claim: Restriction of meningeal lymphatic drainage by ligation has no effect on the total number of cDC1s and cDC2s in the DCLNs.
source: Interestingly, restriction of meningeal lymphatic drainage by ligation had no effect on the total number of cDC1s and cDC2s in the DCLNs (Figure 3b–c) but did result in a reduction in the frequency and number of CD103+ cDC1 s and CD103+ cDC2s at this site (Figure 3d–i), consistent with a migratory function for this subset of dendritic cells (Merad et al., 2013; Mildner and Jung, 2014).
evidence: Supported by spectral flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3b-c

claim: Ligation results in a reduction in the frequency and number of CD103+ cDC1s and CD103+ cDC2s in the DCLNs.
source: Interestingly, restriction of meningeal lymphatic drainage by ligation had no effect on the total number of cDC1s and cDC2s in the DCLNs (Figure 3b–c) but did result in a reduction in the frequency and number of CD103+ cDC1 s and CD103+ cDC2s at this site (Figure 3d–i), consistent with a migratory function for this subset of dendritic cells (Merad et al., 2013; Mildner and Jung, 2014).
evidence: Supported by spectral flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3d-i

claim: Expression of co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 by both cDC1s and cDC2s is significantly reduced after ligation.
source: Additionally, even though there was no difference in the overall number of cDC1s and cDC2s in the DCLNs, the expression of co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 by both cDC1s and cDC2s was significantly reduced after ligation (Figure 3j–q).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 3j-q

claim: Restricting meningeal lymphatic outflow leads to a significant decrease in the frequency and number of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressing CD69 in the DCLNs.
source: Indeed, restricting meningeal lymphatic outflow led to a significant decrease in the frequency and number of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs expressing the early activation marker CD69, despite equal numbers of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells being present in the lymph nodes after ligation (Figure 4a–b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-f).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4a-b and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-f

claim: Ligation causes a decrease in expression of CD69 by SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs.
source: Similarly, when Pru-OVA was used to infect mice, ligation caused a decrease in expression of CD69 by SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4c-d

claim: Ligation results in a concomitant decrease in the frequency of proliferative CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs.
source: To assess whether this decrease in activation was associated with reduced T cell proliferation, we measured Ki67 expression by flow cytometry and observed a concomitant decrease in the frequency of proliferative CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in ligated mice (Figure 4e–h).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4e-h

claim: IFN-γ production is reduced by 69% among CD4+ T cells and 60% among CD8+ T cells in the DCLNs after ligation surgery.
source: Remarkably, IFN-γ production was reduced by 69% among CD4+ T cells and 60% among CD8+ T cells after ligation surgery (Figure 4i–n).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figures 4i-n

claim: TNF-α production is impaired in CD4+ T cells isolated from the DCLNs of ligated mice.
source: TNF-α production was similarly impaired in CD4+ T cells isolated from the DCLNs of ligated mice (Figure 4o–q).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figures 4o-q

claim: Restricting meningeal lymphatic drainage has no discernible impact on the magnitude or quality of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in the brain.
source: Unexpectedly, restricting meningeal lymphatic drainage had no discernible impact on the magnitude or quality of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in the brain after ligation, despite impairing T cell responses in the deep cervical lymph nodes (Figure 5a–e).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5a-e

claim: The total number of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the brain remains unchanged between sham and ligated mice.
source: Indeed, the total number of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the brain remained unchanged between sham and ligated mice (Figure 5a–b), and the frequency of activated (CD44hiCD62Llo) cells did not change (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5a-b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-d

claim: The total number of IFN-γ-producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the brain following ex vivo restimulation with STAg does not change after ligation.
source: To determine whether there were differences in the quality of T cell responses in the brain, we measured the total number of IFN-γ-producing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the brain following ex vivo restimulation with STAg, but again saw no change after ligation (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figures 5c-d

claim: No differences are detected in the total number of SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cells in the brains of sham-operated or ligated mice chronically infected with Pru-OVA.
source: Finally, no differences were detected in the total number of SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cells in the brains of sham-operated or ligated mice chronically infected with Pru-OVA (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 5e

claim: Parasite burden is similar between sham-operated and ligated mice.
source: Because parasite burden was similar between the two groups (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 1e), it is unlikely that any other mechanism of parasite control became defective in the brain as a consequence of ligation.
evidence: Supported by real-time PCR and cyst count data shown in Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1e

claim: A large percentage of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells express Ki67 in the DCLNs at 6 weeks post-infection, indicating robust T cell proliferation.
source: A large percentage of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells expressed Ki67 in the DCLNs at this time point, indicating robust T cell proliferation in CNS-draining lymph nodes during chronic brain infection (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 flow cytometry data shown in Figures 6a-d

claim: A large population of Ki67-expressing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells is detected in the ILNs at 6 weeks post-infection, albeit at a lower frequency than in the DCLNs.
source: Interestingly, though, a large population of Ki67-expressing CD4+ and CD8+ T cells was also detected in the ILNs at this time point, albeit at a lower frequency (Figure 6a–d).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 flow cytometry data shown in Figures 6a-d

claim: 46% of OT-I cells display complete CellTrace Violet dilution in the DCLNs when mice are infected with Pru-OVA, compared to only 11% when infected with parental Pru.
source: Notably, 46% of OT-I cells displayed complete dilution in the DCLNs when mice were infected with Pru-OVA, compared to only 11% of OT-I cells when mice were infected with parental Pru (Figure 6i–j).
evidence: Supported by CellTrace Violet dilution data shown in Figures 6i-j

claim: 51% of OT-I cells fully dilute CellTrace Violet tracer dye in the ILNs of mice infected with Pru-OVA compared to 8% in mice infected with parental Pru.
source: Intriguingly, the degree of antigen-dependent T cell proliferation at this site was similar to that observed in the deep cervical lymph nodes, as 51% of OT-I cells fully diluted the tracer dye in mice infected with Pru-OVA compared to 8% of OT-I cells in mice infected with parental Pru (Figure 6k–l).
evidence: Supported by CellTrace Violet dilution data shown in Figures 6k-l

claim: Antigenic stimulation of T cells occurs concurrently in CNS- and non-CNS-draining lymph nodes during chronic infection.
source: These data lead us to conclude that antigenic stimulation of T cells occurs concurrently in CNS- and non-CNS-draining lymph nodes during chronic infection.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CellTrace Violet dilution experiments showing antigen-dependent proliferation in both DCLNs and ILNs

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels are observed in rodents, primates, and humans.
source: Meningeal lymphatic vessels are observed in rodents, primates, and humans (Absinta et al., 2017; Albayram et al., 2022), and in experimental models of brain cancer and autoimmunity these vessels have been shown to play an integral role in regulating T cell responses in the CNS (Song et al., 2020; Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Absinta et al., 2017 and Albayram et al., 2022

claim: In experimental models of brain cancer and autoimmunity, meningeal lymphatic vessels play an integral role in regulating T cell responses in the CNS.
source: Meningeal lymphatic vessels are observed in rodents, primates, and humans (Absinta et al., 2017; Albayram et al., 2022), and in experimental models of brain cancer and autoimmunity these vessels have been shown to play an integral role in regulating T cell responses in the CNS (Song et al., 2020; Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Song et al., 2020 and Louveau et al., 2018b

claim: T cells play an essential role in orchestrating host-protective immune responses in the CNS during infection.
source: Although the presence of T cells in the CNS can be pathological, T cells play an essential role in orchestrating host-protective immune responses in the CNS during infection (Ellwardt et al., 2016; Korn and Kallies, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ellwardt et al., 2016 and Korn and Kallies, 2017

claim: Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular protozoan parasite that causes chronic, lifelong infection in a wide range of mammalian hosts, including humans.
source: One well-studied brain-tropic pathogen is Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular protozoan parasite that causes chronic, lifelong infection in a wide range of mammalian hosts, including humans (Hill and Dubey, 2002; Pappas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hill and Dubey, 2002 and Pappas et al., 2009

claim: Severe neurologic disease from T. gondii can manifest in immunocompromised individuals, including HIV/AIDS patients.
source: Although the course of infection is typically asymptomatic in humans, severe neurologic disease can manifest in immunocompromised individuals, including HIV/AIDS patients (Luft and Remington, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luft and Remington, 1992

claim: Mice deficient in T cell responses are unable to protect the host from fatal T. gondii disease.
source: Consistent with this susceptibility, experimental studies have demonstrated that mice deficient in T cell responses are unable to protect the host from fatal disease (Gazzinelli et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gazzinelli et al., 1992

claim: Parasite-specific T cells are actively and continuously recruited to the brain in response to T. gondii infection.
source: At homeostasis, the immunologically quiescent brain harbors very few T cells, but in response to T. gondii infection, parasite-specific T cells are actively and continuously recruited to the brain (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2012

claim: Circulating T cells that have been activated in the periphery can only persist within the brain when their cognate antigen is expressed in the brain.
source: The process is tightly regulated, as circulating T cells that have been activated in the periphery can only persist within the brain when their cognate antigen is expressed in the brain (Schaeffer et al., 2009; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schaeffer et al., 2009 and Wilson et al., 2009

claim: Disrupting entry of newly activated T cells into the brain leads to impaired parasite restriction.
source: Disrupting entry of newly activated T cells into the brain leads to impaired parasite restriction, indicating that ongoing T cell stimulation in the periphery is essential (Harris et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2012 and Wilson et al., 2009

claim: The brain parenchyma does not harbor lymphatic vessels.
source: However, because the brain parenchyma does not harbor lymphatic vessels, it remains poorly understood how peripheral T cells become alerted to the presence of microbial antigen in the brain.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about the brain

claim: Lymphatic vessels serve as conduits for the transport of tissue-derived antigen and dendritic cells to lymph nodes in other organs.
source: In other organs, lymphatic vessels serve as conduits for the transport of tissue-derived antigen and dendritic cells to lymph nodes, where naive and memory T cells are optimally positioned for detection of their cognate antigen (Thomas et al., 2016; Gasteiger et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thomas et al., 2016 and Gasteiger et al., 2016

claim: Functional lymphatic vessels have been discovered in the dura mater layer of meninges.
source: The recent discovery of functional lymphatic vessels in the dura mater layer of meninges has prompted a significant reconsideration of how the CNS engages the peripheral immune system (Louveau et al., 2015b; Aspelund et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Louveau et al., 2015b and Aspelund et al., 2015

claim: When model antigens like ovalbumin are injected into the brain, these molecules travel from the brain interstitium into the CSF via glymphatic flow.
source: Indeed, when model antigens like ovalbumin (OVA) are injected into the brain, these molecules travel from the brain interstitium into the CSF via glymphatic flow (Iliff et al., 2012) and have the potential to be presented to T cells in the deep cervical lymph nodes (Ling et al., 2003; Harris et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iliff et al., 2012

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage contributes to the clearance of Japanese encephalitis virus from the brain and promotes host survival in a murine model of acute brain infection.
source: In a murine model of acute brain infection, it was shown that meningeal lymphatic drainage contributes to the clearance of Japanese encephalitis virus from the brain and promotes host survival (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2022

claim: The dura mater layer of meninges has emerged as an important anatomic site for immune surveillance of the CNS.
source: The dura mater layer of meninges has emerged as an important anatomic site for immune surveillance of the CNS (Alves de Lima et al., 2020; Rua and McGavern, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alves de Lima et al., 2020 and Rua and McGavern, 2018

claim: Soluble brain- and CSF-derived molecules accumulate within the meninges around the dural sinuses and can be captured by local antigen-presenting cells.
source: Soluble brain- and CSF-derived molecules accumulate within the meninges around the dural sinuses and can be captured by local antigen-presenting cells (APCs) (Louveau et al., 2018b; Rustenhoven et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Louveau et al., 2018b and Rustenhoven et al., 2021

claim: The dural meninges develop an extensive network of lymphatic vessels which directly transport soluble brain- and CSF-derived molecules to peripheral lymph nodes.
source: Moreover, in contrast to the brain, which is devoid of lymphatic vessels, the dural meninges develop an extensive network of lymphatic vessels which directly transport soluble brain- and CSF-derived molecules to peripheral lymph nodes (Aspelund et al., 2015; Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aspelund et al., 2015 and Louveau et al., 2018b

claim: At homeostasis, a small number of APCs in the dural meninges surround lymphatic vessels, and upon stimulation these cells can traffic to the deep cervical lymph nodes.
source: At homeostasis, a small number of APCs in the dural meninges surround these lymphatic vessels, and upon stimulation these cells can traffic to the deep cervical lymph nodes (Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Louveau et al., 2018b

claim: CD11chiMHC IIhi APCs accumulate in the brain during T. gondii infection.
source: Although CD11chiMHC IIhi APCs accumulate in the brain during T. gondii infection (John et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2000), there is only limited evidence to suggest that, in the absence of local lymphatic vasculature, these cells are able to migrate out of the brain to transport antigen directly to peripheral lymph nodes (Carare et al., 2008; Clarkson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to John et al., 2011 and Fischer et al., 2000

claim: There is only limited evidence that APCs in the brain can migrate out to transport antigen directly to peripheral lymph nodes in the absence of local lymphatic vasculature.
source: Although CD11chiMHC IIhi APCs accumulate in the brain during T. gondii infection (John et al., 2011; Fischer et al., 2000), there is only limited evidence to suggest that, in the absence of local lymphatic vasculature, these cells are able to migrate out of the brain to transport antigen directly to peripheral lymph nodes (Carare et al., 2008; Clarkson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Carare et al., 2008 and Clarkson et al., 2017

claim: Professional APCs in the dural meninges are uniquely positioned to sample CNS material and traffic through lymphatic vessels to lymph nodes for T cell activation.
source: By contrast, professional APCs in the dural meninges are uniquely positioned to sample CNS material and traffic through lymphatic vessels to lymph nodes for T cell activation.
evidence: Logical inference based on anatomical positioning and known functions of APCs and lymphatic vessels

claim: Chronic brain infection promotes maturation of dendritic cells in the dural meninges but has a greater effect on the activation status of cDC2s than cDC1s.
source: These data suggest that chronic brain infection promotes maturation of dendritic cells in the dural meninges but has a greater effect on the activation status of cDC2s than cDC1s.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from flow cytometry data showing differential upregulation of activation markers

claim: The accumulation of cDC1s and cDC2s in the dural meninges occurred independently of ongoing infection of the dural meninges.
source: These data suggest that the accumulation of cDC1s and cDC2s in the dural meninges occurred independently of ongoing infection of the dural meninges.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that parasite was not detected in dural meninges despite DC accumulation

claim: Immune cells at border tissues of the CNS, including the dural meninges, play a key role in responding to pathology within the brain parenchyma.
source: This finding reinforces an emerging view that immune cells at border tissues of the CNS, including the dural meninges, play a key role in responding to pathology within the brain parenchyma (Alves de Lima et al., 2020; Rua and McGavern, 2018; Rustenhoven et al., 2021; Cugurra et al., 2021; Pulous et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alves de Lima et al., 2020; Rua and McGavern, 2018; Rustenhoven et al., 2021; Cugurra et al., 2021; Pulous et al., 2022

claim: Activated dendritic cells introduced into the CSF exit the CNS by accessing meningeal lymphatic vessels.
source: Because activated dendritic cells introduced into the CSF exit the CNS by accessing meningeal lymphatic vessels (Louveau et al., 2018b), it is possible that some of the dendritic cells that we observed in the meninges of infected mice came from the CSF.
evidence: Supported by citation to Louveau et al., 2018b

claim: The concentration of CSF-borne APCs in chronically infected mice is consistent with that reported in human CSF samples from patients with Lyme neuroborreliosis.
source: Interestingly, the concentration of CSF-borne APCs was consistent with that reported by a study of human CSF samples isolated from patients with Lyme neuroborreliosis (Pashenkov et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pashenkov et al., 2001

claim: CSF functions as a sink for brain-derived macromolecules.
source: CSF has been shown to function as a sink for brain-derived macromolecules (Abbott, 2004; Plog and Nedergaard, 2018) and capturing CSF-borne protein represents a potential mechanism by which APCs in the dural meninges could sample brain-derived antigen and transport it to lymph nodes in the periphery.
evidence: Supported by citations to Abbott, 2004 and Plog and Nedergaard, 2018

claim: DQ-OVA is a self-quenched conjugate of ovalbumin labeled with BODIPY dyes that only emits fluorescence after proteolytic cleavage.
source: DQ-OVA is a self-quenched conjugate of ovalbumin labeled with BODIPY dyes that only emits fluorescence after proteolytic cleavage.
evidence: Description of the properties of the DQ-OVA reagent

claim: DQ-OVA has been commonly used to examine uptake and processing of soluble antigen by dendritic cells.
source: DQ-OVA has been commonly used to examine uptake and processing of soluble antigen by dendritic cells (Ling et al., 2003; Gerner et al., 2017; Sixt et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ling et al., 2003; Gerner et al., 2017; Sixt et al., 2005

claim: Dural APCs capture and transport CSF-borne antigen during chronic brain infection.
source: Imaging of whole mount dural meninges revealed that DQ-OVA+ cells were distributed along and within lymphatic vessels after 12 hr, suggesting that dural APCs capture and transport CSF-borne antigen during chronic brain infection (Figure 1m).
evidence: Inference based on imaging data showing DQ-OVA+ cells in and around lymphatic vessels

claim: Type 1 and type 2 conventional dendritic cells increased in number in the dural meninges, displayed a more activated phenotype, and were able to sample CSF-borne protein in the vicinity of meningeal lymphatic vessels.
source: All together, these findings highlight significant changes in the APC compartment of the dural meninges in response to T. gondii brain infection. Type 1 and type 2 conventional dendritic cells increased in number in the dural meninges, displayed a more activated phenotype, and were able to sample CSF-borne protein in the vicinity of meningeal lymphatic vessels.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript

claim: Meningeal lymphatic vessels drain directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes in mice and humans.
source: Initial studies in mice, and later in humans, have demonstrated that meningeal lymphatic vessels drain directly to the deep cervical lymph nodes (DCLN) (Albayram et al., 2022; Louveau et al., 2018b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albayram et al., 2022 and Louveau et al., 2018b

claim: Injection of antigen into rodent brains elicited strong humoral responses in the DCLNs.
source: For example, injection of antigen into rodent brains elicited strong humoral responses in the DCLNs (Harling-Berg et al., 1989), and surgical excision of the DCLNs contributed to a reduction in severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (van Zwam et al., 2009; Furtado, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harling-Berg et al., 1989

claim: Surgical excision of the DCLNs contributed to a reduction in severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
source: For example, injection of antigen into rodent brains elicited strong humoral responses in the DCLNs (Harling-Berg et al., 1989), and surgical excision of the DCLNs contributed to a reduction in severity of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (van Zwam et al., 2009; Furtado, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Zwam et al., 2009 and Furtado, 2008

claim: During chronic infection, CSF-derived protein can be sampled by APCs within the deep cervical lymph nodes.
source: To address the role of the DCLNs during T. gondii infection, we first confirmed that during chronic infection CSF-derived protein could be sampled by APCs within these lymph nodes.
evidence: Confirmed by DQ-OVA injection experiments

claim: In peripheral organs, foreign antigen is transported directly from the site of infection to lymph nodes for immune cell activation.
source: In peripheral organs, foreign antigen is transported directly from the site of infection to lymph nodes for immune cell activation (Liao and von der Weid, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liao and von der Weid, 2015

claim: Antigen expressed in infected brain tissue must first reach the cerebrospinal fluid before it can be transported to lymph nodes for T cell activation.
source: However, our data support a model in which antigen expressed in infected brain tissue must first reach the cerebrospinal fluid before it can be transported to lymph nodes for T cell activation.
evidence: Model proposed based on experimental findings showing impaired T cell responses after lymphatic ligation

claim: Lymphatic vessels promote the trafficking of dendritic cells from infected tissue after antigen uptake and phenotypic maturation.
source: In addition to the drainage of soluble antigen, lymphatic vessels promote the trafficking of dendritic cells from infected tissue after antigen uptake and phenotypic maturation (Russo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Russo et al., 2013

claim: cDC1s are critical for initiating Th1 immunity against T. gondii during acute infection.
source: While it is well-established that cDC1s are critical for initiating Th1 immunity against T. gondii during acute infection (Poncet et al., 2019), less is known about the role of cDC1s and cDC2s during chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Poncet et al., 2019

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage is required for dendritic cell responses in the deep cervical lymph nodes during chronic T. gondii infection.
source: These data suggest that in the setting of brain infection meningeal lymphatic drainage promotes maturation of dendritic cells at this site.
evidence: Conclusion based on ligation experiments showing reduced DC maturation markers

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage promotes robust T cell activation, proliferation, and cytokine production in the deep cervical lymph nodes during chronic T. gondii infection.
source: All together, we can conclude that meningeal lymphatic drainage contributes to robust parasite-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in the deep cervical lymph nodes during chronic brain infection.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple T cell functional assays after ligation

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage is host-protective during acute viral infection of the brain.
source: However, in contrast to the finding that meningeal lymphatic drainage is host-protective during acute viral infection of the brain (Li et al., 2022), we observed that meningeal lymphatic drainage is dispensable for controlling T. gondii infection of the brain, with the T cell response in the brain remaining intact following surgical disruption of meningeal lymphatic outflow.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2022

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage is dispensable for controlling T. gondii infection of the brain.
source: However, in contrast to the finding that meningeal lymphatic drainage is host-protective during acute viral infection of the brain (Li et al., 2022), we observed that meningeal lymphatic drainage is dispensable for controlling T. gondii infection of the brain, with the T cell response in the brain remaining intact following surgical disruption of meningeal lymphatic outflow.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no change in brain T cell responses or parasite burden after ligation

claim: Concurrent activation of T cells at alternative sites, including lymph nodes that do not drain the CNS, potentially explains the durability of the T cell response in the brain after lymphatic ligation.
source: Concurrent activation of T cells at alternative sites, including lymph nodes that do not drain the CNS, potentially explains the durability of the T cell response in the brain.
evidence: Proposed explanation based on observation of antigen-dependent T cell proliferation in non-CNS-draining lymph nodes

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage promotes T cell responses against antigen expressed in the brain.
source: Overall, our findings highlight the role of the dural meninges in the immune response to chronic brain infection, providing new evidence that meningeal lymphatic drainage promotes T cell responses against antigen expressed in the brain.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on experimental findings showing impaired T cell responses in DCLNs after ligation

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage is essential for T cell-dependent immunity against brain tumors.
source: By contrast, when tumors originate within the CNS, meningeal lymphatic drainage was found to be indispensable for T cell-dependent immunity in the brain (Song et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020), likely because there were not alternative sources of antigen outside the CNS.
evidence: Supported by citations to Song et al., 2020 and Hu et al., 2020

claim: When tumor cells are injected into the flank at the same time as intracranial engraftment, survival benefits of VEGF-C-enhanced meningeal lymphatic drainage are abrogated.
source: Consistent with this idea, when tumor cells were injected into the flank of mice at the same time as intracranial engraftment, survival benefits of VEGF-C-enhanced meningeal lymphatic drainage were abrogated (Song et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2020

claim: Skin grafts in the brain were rejected more quickly and at higher rates when also engrafted to the chest of rabbits.
source: These results harken back to early studies performed by Medawar in the 1940s showing that skin grafts in the brain were rejected more quickly and at higher rates when also engrafted to the chest of rabbits (Medawar, 1948).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medawar, 1948

claim: Meningeal lymphatic drainage may not be necessary to generate T cell responses against metastatic brain tumors, given the presence of early peripheral antigen prior to seeding of the brain.
source: For these reasons, we predict that meningeal lymphatic drainage may not be necessary to generate T cell responses against metastatic brain tumors, given the presence of early peripheral antigen prior to seeding of the brain.
evidence: Prediction based on the findings that peripheral antigen sources can compensate for loss of CNS lymphatic drainage

claim: Most CNS pathogens display varying degrees of tropism for multiple tissues and originate at a peripheral site prior to hematogenous dissemination to the brain, CSF, or meninges.
source: The presence of peripheral antigen during T. gondii brain infection is not surprising, as most CNS pathogens display varying degrees of tropism for multiple tissues and originate at a peripheral site prior to hematogenous dissemination to the brain, CSF, or meninges (Cain et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cain et al., 2019

claim: Peripheral infection may serve to 'immunize' the host ahead of CNS infection, making the drainage of CNS antigen to the deep cervical lymph nodes more redundant.
source: In fact, peripheral infection may serve to 'immunize' the host ahead of CNS infection, making the drainage of CNS antigen to the deep cervical lymph nodes more redundant.
evidence: Proposed explanation for why meningeal lymphatic drainage is dispensable during T. gondii infection

claim: Residual antigen persisting after clearance of acute infection likely contributes to T cell proliferation in non-CNS-draining lymph nodes during chronic infection.
source: However, considering the robust T cell responses and high levels of parasite gDNA observed in the inguinal lymph nodes during acute infection, it is possible that residual antigen persisting after clearance of acute infection contributed to the proliferation of OT-I cells at this site during chronic infection.
evidence: Speculation based on observed T cell responses and known phenomenon of antigen persistence

claim: Antigen depots can persist for weeks to months after viral clearance in models of influenza or vesicular stomatitis virus infection.
source: In models of influenza or vesicular stomatitis virus infection, antigen depots were found to persist for weeks to months after viral clearance (Turner et al., 2007; Zammit et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Turner et al., 2007 and Zammit et al., 2006

claim: Both CNS-draining lymph nodes and non-CNS-draining lymph nodes are sources of newly activated parasite-specific T cells during the chronic stage of T. gondii infection.
source: In summary, these experiments reveal that both CNS-draining lymph nodes and non-CNS-draining lymph nodes are sources of newly activated parasite-specific T cells during the chronic stage of T. gondii infection.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on CellTrace Violet dilution experiments

claim: Ongoing proliferation of T cells in lymph nodes that do not drain the CNS may explain the durability of T cell responses in the brain when T cell responses in the deep cervical lymph nodes become impaired.
source: Ongoing proliferation of T cells in lymph nodes that do not drain the CNS, such as the inguinal lymph nodes, may explain the durability of T cell responses in the brain when T cell responses in the deep cervical lymph nodes become impaired.
evidence: Proposed explanation based on experimental findings

claim: The dural meninges promote neuroimmune communication during chronic brain infection.
source: To conclude, our study provides novel insight into how T cells respond to antigen expressed in the brain by a neurotropic pathogen. Our data shed new light on how the dural meninges promotes neuroimmune communication, while refining our understanding of how meningeal lymphatic drainage helps to preserve the health of the CNS.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on overall findings of the study

claim: CD103+ dendritic cell subsets have a migratory function.
source: Interestingly, restriction of meningeal lymphatic drainage by ligation had no effect on the total number of cDC1s and cDC2s in the DCLNs (Figure 3b–c) but did result in a reduction in the frequency and number of CD103+ cDC1 s and CD103+ cDC2s at this site (Figure 3d–i), consistent with a migratory function for this subset of dendritic cells (Merad et al., 2013; Mildner and Jung, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Merad et al., 2013 and Mildner and Jung, 2014

claim: T cell activation in the superficial cervical lymph nodes is not affected by ligation of vessels draining to the DCLNs.
source: Of note, T cell activation in the superficial cervical lymph nodes, which drain facial tissues and serve as an additional drainage site for CSF (Ma et al., 2017; Lohrberg and Wilting, 2016), was not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1g-i).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1g-i and citations to Ma et al., 2017 and Lohrberg and Wilting, 2016

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cells confer protection to the host during T. gondii infection by producing large amounts of IFN-γ and TNF-α.
source: During T. gondii infection, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells confer protection to the host by producing large amounts of IFN-γ and TNF-α, cytokines that activate intracellular mechanisms of parasite restriction in infected host cells (Schlüter et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schlüter et al., 2003 and Wang et al., 2004

claim: IFN-γ and TNF-α are cytokines that activate intracellular mechanisms of parasite restriction in infected host cells.
source: During T. gondii infection, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells confer protection to the host by producing large amounts of IFN-γ and TNF-α, cytokines that activate intracellular mechanisms of parasite restriction in infected host cells (Schlüter et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schlüter et al., 2003 and Wang et al., 2004

claim: T cell responses are parasite-specific as indicated by lack of IFN-γ and TNF-α production in unstimulated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: IFN-γ and TNF-α production was not detected in unstimulated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, suggesting that T cell responses were parasite-specific (Figure 4j, m and p).
evidence: Supported by intracellular cytokine staining data showing no cytokine production without antigen stimulation

claim: The T cell population in the brain requires continual replenishment by circulating T cells during T. gondii infection.
source: Because the T cell population in the brain requires continual replenishment by circulating T cells (Harris et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2009), these results suggest that alternative sources of antigen likely exist outside the CNS-draining lymph nodes during chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris et al., 2012 and Wilson et al., 2009

claim: T cell proliferation is enriched in lymph nodes that drain CNS tissue at 6 weeks post-infection when parasite is most abundant in the brain.
source: These data suggest that T cell proliferation is enriched in lymph nodes that drain CNS tissue at 6 wpi, when parasite is most abundant in the brain, but also occurs in lymph nodes that do not drain CNS tissue.
evidence: Conclusion based on Ki67 expression data in DCLNs and ILNs

claim: Proliferation of SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cells in CNS-draining lymph nodes is predominantly antigen-dependent.
source: These data indicate that proliferation of SIINFEKL-specific CD8+ T cells in CNS-draining lymph nodes is predominantly antigen-dependent, and only a limited degree of proliferation can be attributed to bystander activation.
evidence: Conclusion based on CellTrace Violet dilution data comparing Pru-OVA and parental Pru infection

claim: All OT-I cells detected in the brains of Pru-OVA infected mice had fully diluted their CellTrace Violet dye.
source: As expected, OT-I cells only accumulated in the brains of mice infected with Pru-OVA (Figure 6f–g), and all of the OT-I cells detected in the brains of these mice had fully diluted their CellTrace Violet dye (Figure 6h), consistent with the notion that these cells undergo several rounds of proliferation prior to recruitment to the brain.
evidence: Supported by CellTrace Violet dilution data shown in Figure 6h

claim: OT-I cells undergo several rounds of proliferation prior to recruitment to the brain.
source: As expected, OT-I cells only accumulated in the brains of mice infected with Pru-OVA (Figure 6f–g), and all of the OT-I cells detected in the brains of these mice had fully diluted their CellTrace Violet dye (Figure 6h), consistent with the notion that these cells undergo several rounds of proliferation prior to recruitment to the brain.
evidence: Inference based on complete CellTrace Violet dilution observed in brain-infiltrating OT-I cells
